vignette:
Marcus

Marcus stands in his restaurant kitchen at five in the morning, moving through prep work with the precision of someone who has done this ten thousand times. His hands move automatically-dicing onions, portioning proteins, arranging mise en place-while his mind exists somewhere else entirely. He is fifty-three kilometers from the border, listening to the sound of shells landing in the neighborhood where his cousin still lives. No. He is in his kitchen in Toronto. The sound is the walk-in freezer compressor. He steadies himself against the counter and takes three deliberate breaths.

At forty-four, Marcus has been in Canada for sixteen years. He arrived with nothing but his knowledge of how to cook-the one thing the war couldn't take from him. In Afghanistan, before everything collapsed, he had owned a small restaurant in Kabul with his brother. They served traditional Afghan cuisine to families and businessmen. Marcus had trained under his father, who had trained under his grandfather. It was not just work; it was identity, continuity, a way of honoring something ancient and good.

The evacuation came suddenly. One day there was talk of the Taliban advancing, and the next day Marcus was running. His brother had stayed behind to help their mother. Marcus has not heard from either of them in seven years. He does not let himself think about why.

He built his current restaurant slowly, working first as a line cook, then as sous chef, saving every dollar. The restaurant is small but respected-a place where people come for authenticity, for the flavors of home. His staff respects him. He is exacting but fair. They do not know that when the dinner rush reaches its peak and the kitchen fills with heat and noise and urgency, Marcus sometimes feels the walls closing in. They do not see him step into the walk-in freezer not for ingredients but to breathe cold air and remind himself that he is safe.

Sleep has become a negotiation. Marcus goes to bed around midnight and wakes at three or four in the morning, his heart racing, his shirt soaked through. Sometimes he remembers the dreams-running through dark streets, searching for his brother's face in crowds of strangers. More often, he simply finds himself awake in the dark, hypervigilant, listening to the sounds of the sleeping city and cataloging threats that do not exist. He has tried everything: herbal tea, meditation videos, even medication from a doctor who seemed uncomfortable discussing why he needed it. Nothing works reliably.

During the day, unexpected things trigger a flood of panic. A siren sends him back to Kabul. A news report about Afghanistan makes his chest tight for hours. Last month, a customer raised his voice about a late order, and Marcus found himself unable to respond, frozen, while his manager handled the situation. Afterward, he sat in his office for twenty minutes, ashamed and confused by his own reaction.

He has friends-other Afghans who understand without needing explanation, colleagues from the restaurant who value his work. But he keeps distance from all of them. Relationships require vulnerability, and Marcus has learned that vulnerability is dangerous. He has learned that the people you love can disappear. So he comes to his kitchen, where he can control the variables, where he can create something beautiful and sustaining, where the work is honest and the outcomes are predictable. He comes here at five in the morning and he stays until the last plate is served and the kitchen is clean.

He is still running, though he has not moved in years.
